# The four case studies {#the-four-cases .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Section 3
:::

::: notes
This section brings the programme down to the workshop's four case studies, each a claim that went through the robustness study and, to different degrees, through the rest of SCORE. We read the four claims as the analysts received them, then the conclusions of the five analysts of each claim side by side, and then the record of each case study across the three Rs. Your own case study is one of the four, and since you meet it properly on the second day, the aim for now is only to place it among the others.
:::

## The four claims {#the-four-claims .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Case study | The study | The claim, as the robustness study gave it |
|:----|:-------------|:-------------|
| Housing and racial bias | A field experiment of 2017: one email to each of about a thousand public housing authorities in the United States, signed with names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic sender | "Hispanic housing applicants were ... less likely to be greeted by name than were ... white counterparts" |
| Immigration and trust | An analysis of 2012 of rounds 1 to 4 of the European Social Survey, in 16 Western European countries | "... concerns about the effect of immigration on the national community have a(n) [reducing] impact on trust in politics" |
| Cohabitation and marriage | An analysis of 2016 of the first cohabitations of American women, begun in the early 1990s and in the late 2000s, from the National Survey of Family Growth | "cohabitors have increasingly become less likely to progress to marriage" |
| Europeanisation and the economy | An analysis of 2016 of sixteen Eurobarometer waves, 2004 to 2013, in 27 member states of the European Union | "... poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" |
:::

::: {.src}
@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, abstract; @McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope, p. 199; @KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion, p. 932; @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619.
:::

::: notes
These are the four claims in the form in which the robustness study handed them to the analysts, with the dots and the square brackets of the lead team left in. The Housing claim is the only one of the four that comes from an experiment, emails to public housing authorities in the United States that differed only in the name that signed them. The Immigration claim comes from the European Social Survey, the Cohabitation claim from the union histories of American women, and the Europeanisation claim from sixteen waves of the Eurobarometer. The claims are worth reading for what they leave out as much as for what they say: the Housing claim, for instance, states a direction and no size, because an ellipsis removed the twenty percentage points of the abstract.
:::

## The conclusions of the analysts {#the-conclusions-of-the-analysts}

```{r}
#| label: four-case-conclusions
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.3
# The Task 1 conclusions of the five analysts of the robustness study for each
# case study, as the page score.qmd of this site states them (section "The four
# case studies in the record"), from the facts file of each case study. One tile
# per analyst, in no particular order within a case study.
conclusions <- tibble::tribble(
  ~case,             ~conclusion,                  ~n,
  "Housing",         "Evidence for the claim",     3,
  "Housing",         "No evidence either way",     2,
  "Immigration",     "Evidence for the claim",     5,
  "Cohabitation",    "Evidence for the claim",     2,
  "Cohabitation",    "No evidence either way",     1,
  "Cohabitation",    "Evidence for the opposite",  2,
  "Europeanisation", "Evidence for the claim",     5
) |>
  tidyr::uncount(n) |>
  dplyr::mutate(analyst = dplyr::row_number(), .by = case) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    case = factor(case, levels = rev(c("Housing", "Immigration",
                                       "Cohabitation", "Europeanisation"))),
    conclusion = factor(conclusion, levels = c("Evidence for the claim",
                                               "No evidence either way",
                                               "Evidence for the opposite"))
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(conclusions, ggplot2::aes(analyst, case, fill = conclusion)) +
  ggplot2::geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 3, width = 0.96, height = 0.82) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, grey_mid, d_red), name = NULL) +
  # without the white border of the tiles, which would cover the legend keys
  ggplot2::guides(fill = ggplot2::guide_legend(override.aes = list(colour = NA))) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.05)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(16) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom",
                 legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 13, colour = ink),
                 legend.key.size = ggplot2::unit(1.1, "lines"),
                 panel.grid = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_blank(),
                 axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink, size = 17))
```

::: {.small}
Every analyst upheld the Immigration and the Europeanisation claims, while the partial correlations recorded for those ten reanalyses run from 0.122 to 0.198 and from −0.006 to −0.452.
:::

::: {.src}
The Task 1 conclusions recorded in the robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], as the page SCORE and the opening page of the workshop's website state them.
:::

::: notes
Each row is one case study and each tile one analyst, coloured by the conclusion recorded in the first task. All five analysts upheld the Immigration and the Europeanisation claims. The Housing claim split three to two, with the other two analysts finding evidence neither way, and the Cohabitation claim split three ways, two for, one neither way and two for the opposite, all of them working on the file that the robustness study gave them. Agreement on the conclusion, however, is a different matter from agreement on the number: the Immigration analysts recorded correlations within a narrow band, while those of the Europeanisation analysts span nearly two orders of magnitude, for the reason shown by the slide on what the conversion assumes.
:::

## The four case studies in the record {#the-four-cases-in-the-record .smaller}

::: {.fs-75}
| Case study | Reproduction | Robustness | Replication |
|:----|:----------|:---------|:----------|
| Housing | never attempted, although the data and code are public | 3 of the 5 analysts for the claim, 2 neither way | a new preregistered experiment with 3,050 housing authorities found no significant gap |
| Immigration | two reproductions from the survey files, close to the published coefficient but on fewer respondents | all 5 for the claim | two replications on later rounds of the survey, both meeting the criterion of SCORE |
| Cohabitation | none recorded | 2 for the claim, 1 neither way, 2 the opposite | tested another coefficient of the paper, which did not replicate |
| Europeanisation | two attempts from the original materials, neither successful | all 5 for the claim | on later Eurobarometer waves, judged not successful |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Read across the rows. The Europeanisation claim, upheld by every analyst, could be neither reproduced nor replicated, while the Immigration claim, upheld as consistently, replicated.
:::

::: {.src}
The page SCORE on the workshop's website, from the facts file of each case study.
:::

::: notes
This is the whole record across the three Rs. In the reproduction column, one reproduction was never attempted although everything needed for it was public, one was never recorded, two came close on fewer respondents, and two failed. [advance] Read across the rows, the Europeanisation claim, upheld by every one of its analysts, could be neither reproduced from its original materials nor replicated on later waves of its survey, while the Immigration claim, upheld just as consistently, replicated on later rounds of the European Social Survey. Four case studies are far too few for a conclusion about the literature, but they show, one case at a time, why the workshop keeps the three questions apart.
:::
